claims.text: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a controlled nanoscale nickel layer improves bonding between tungsten and copper.
Improved W–Cu interfacial bonding reduces interfacial thermal resistance.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance increases the effective thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
A conventional W–Cu composite has tungsten particles in direct contact with the copper matrix.
A thin interfacial nickel layer improves the wetting of tungsten by copper.
Improved wetting and bonding reduce interfacial voids and defects.
Interfacial thermal barriers and microstructural defects impede electron and phonon transport.
Reducing interfacial thermal barriers and defects enhances electron and phonon transport through the composite.
The nickel layer reinforces the W–Cu interface.
Reinforcement of the interface contributes to sustained mechanical integrity.
Reinforcement of the interface contributes to irradiation resistance.
The nickel-coated W–Cu composite will have significantly higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The nickel-coated composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to that of the uncoated composite.
The nickel-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the uncoated composite.
The predicted benefits apply under elevated temperature, mechanical cycling, and irradiation environments typical of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
An optimized nanoscale nickel thickness can prevent formation of brittle intermetallic phases.
Keeping the nickel layer at an optimized nanoscale thickness preserves the composite's intrinsic mechanical and irradiation-resistant properties.
The magnitude of the conductivity improvement and the optimal coating thickness may depend on processing and operating conditions.
